title: Aksumite gold coin of King Ezanas
language_note: British Museum catalogue record in English; Aksumite coin legends are typically in Greek (for gold/silver issues aimed at external trade) or Ge'ez, not transcribed in this record.
findspot: Found/acquired in Yemen, ~300km north of Aden; minted at Aksum

findspot_places.name: Yemen, roughly 300 km north of Aden
findspot_places.note: The record fixes the findspot as a distance and a bearing from Aden, not as a place. Searched against the Pleiades places snapshot of 2026-08-10: Pleiades 39269 is Aden itself (Adane/Athenae/Eudaimon Arabia, 12.772/45.039) and is roughly 300 km AWAY from where this coin was found, so it is deliberately NOT used — a resolving id at the wrong place is worse than no id. No Pleiades feature covers the intended area at this resolution, so nothing is drawn.

origin_places.name: Aksum
origin_places.note: The record states the coin was minted at Aksum. Confirmed against the Pleiades places snapshot of 2026-08-10 by coordinate — 14.134, 38.721, Tigray — feature types 'cultural-landscape, settlement', attested -30..2100; Pleiades titles it 'A(u)xoume'. This is the same id used as the FINDSPOT of africa-01-ezana-stone; here it is the place of manufacture, which is why the two are separate blocks. Aksum to Yemen is this object's journey, and it is the connection the record exists to document.

original_text_excerpt: Gold coin. Half-length bust of Ezanas right, crowned, holding stick or sceptre, flanked by two wheat-stalks, the whole in a beaded circle. Half-length bust of Ezanas right, wearing headcloth, holding branch (?) or stick, flanked by two wheat-stalks, the whole in a beaded circle.
original_text_note: British Museum catalogue description used as the artefact record.
notes: Aksum was one of only a handful of ancient states to strike its own gold coinage (alongside Rome, Persia, and the Kushan Empire) — itself a signal of engagement with the Roman-dominated Red Sea gold-trade economy. This specimen's findspot in Yemen, not Ethiopia, is a direct data point for Aksum-Arabia contact (pairs with the Sabaic/Himyarite material in the Arabia cluster). Ezana's later coinage replaced the pagan disc-and-crescent with a cross — possibly the earliest use of the Christian cross on any coinage anywhere — a good fact to verify against a second source before use in an answer.
